title.en: The Holocaust and the new international order
From a terrible war to a promise

text.en: In 1945 the world looked at the ruins and asked how such horror could be prevented again. The answer was a promise written on paper by 51 nations: the Charter of the United Nations.

After Hitler came to power the Jews were persecuted, deprived of their civil rights, robbed of their property and confined to ghettos.
The Nazis then planned the Final Solution, which meant destroying the Jews completely.
The word holocaust describes the killing of nearly six million Jews by the Germans during World War II.
Hitler played on the anti-Jewish feeling, anti-Semitism, which was common in Germany and across Europe.
Jews were scattered across Europe and many were prominent in business, the performing arts and the professions, and the fact that money-lending was a major Jewish business deepened prejudice.
By 1941 the United States and Britain were thinking seriously about international cooperation for lasting peace and for economic and financial stability.
The first step was the Atlantic Charter of 1941, a joint declaration by the United States and Britain, which all 26 countries fighting the Axis accepted on New Year's Day 1942.
The Charter of the United Nations was signed on 26 June 1945 by 51 nations, and India, not yet independent, was also a signatory.
Today the United Nations has 193 member states and each, big or small, has an equal vote.
The preamble of the Charter speaks of saving later generations from the scourge of war and of faith in human rights and the equal rights of men and women and of large and small nations.
In the aftermath of the Holocaust the Charter pledged respect for human rights for all without distinction of race, sex, language or religion, and a Commission on Human Rights was formed.
A committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, widow of President Franklin Roosevelt, with members such as Charles Malik, P.C. Chang, John Humphrey and Rene Cassin, drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
The Declaration sets out basic rights in 30 articles, was adopted on 10 December 1948, and that day is observed as Human Rights Day.
About ninety national constitutions since 1948 contain provisions that can be traced to this Declaration.
A major outcome of the Holocaust was the creation of the state of Israel as a homeland for the Jews.
The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund were also created as forums for countries large and small.

problem.en: Explain how the Holocaust influenced the creation of human rights law.

text.en: The Nazis killed nearly six million Jews in the Holocaust.

why.en: The world was shocked by the scale of the crime.

text.en: The UN Charter pledged respect for human rights without distinction of race, sex, language or religion.

why.en: The UN formed a Commission on Human Rights.

text.en: Its committee, chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, produced the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted on 10 December 1948.

why.en: It has 30 articles and inspired about ninety constitutions.

prompt.en: Trace the steps from the Atlantic Charter to the United Nations Charter.

requiredIdeas.en: Atlantic Charter in 1941 by the United States and Britain
26 countries accepted the Declaration of the United Nations on 1 January 1942
The UN Charter was signed on 26 June 1945 by 51 nations

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the UN Charter was signed in 1942
Thinking India could not sign because it was not free

points.en: Holocaust: Final Solution, nearly six million Jews killed.
UN: Atlantic Charter 1941, Charter signed 26 June 1945 by 51 nations; now 193 members.
UDHR: 30 articles, 10 December 1948, Eleanor Roosevelt's committee.
Israel created; World Bank and IMF founded.
